name: Ernie's Walk
text:
Ernie's Walk

Ernie's Walk is a 0.3-mile (0.48 km) linear trail along the north bank of the Los Angeles River in Sherman Oaks, Los Angeles, California. The trail runs along Valleyheart Drive between Kester Avenue and Cedros Avenue. The trail is named for Ernie La Mere, a retired Sherman Oaks resident who began planting along a degraded stretch of riverbank in 1987. Los Angeles County renovated the site in 2003, and it reopened as a county park in 2004.

name: Ernie's Walk
text:
Ernie's Walk › History › Origins

In the late 1980s, the stretch of the Los Angeles River passing through Sherman Oaks near the junction of the Ventura and San Diego freeways had become infiltrated with weeds. It was also used as an illegal dumping ground. Ernie La Mere, a retired local resident, contacted governmental agencies to have the area cleaned up. He began planting extra flowers in the newly cleared riverbank. Some neighbors joined him; the group planted trees and shrubs along the channel. La Mere added some benches and established a section called "Boot Hill," a mock graveyard with humorous epitaphs that eventually came to include pet memorials. A neighbor put up a sign naming the path Ernie's Walk.

La Mere died in 1995. His grandson and some neighbors continued tending the site afterward, though less consistently.

name: Ernie's Walk
text:
Ernie's Walk › History › County renovation

In 2003, the Los Angeles County Department of Public Works renovated the site. Native plants including cottonwood trees were added, and many of La Mere's surviving plants were moved from the water's edge to allow maintenance access. River rock retaining walls, stairs, a ramp, and new fencing were installed. The original wooden "Boot Hill" markers were removed and replaced with a concrete marker inscribed Ernie's Walk Pet Commemorative.

name: Ernie's Walk
text:
Ernie's Walk › Legacy

Ernie's Walk is noted in accounts of the Los Angeles River revitalization movement as an early example of community initiated greening along the concrete channel. The movement grew through the late 1980s and 1990s, including through the work of Friends of the Los Angeles River, founded by poet and activist Lewis MacAdams in 1986. The Los Angeles City Council adopted the Los Angeles River Revitalization Master Plan in 2007.

The site was featured in an episode of the PBS television program Visiting... with Huell Howser. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Works lists it as a stop on its Los Angeles River Watershed Tour.

name: The Epitaph Project
text:
The Epitaph Project

The Epitaph Project is an interactive public art installation located at Hollywood Forever Cemetery in Los Angeles, established in 1995 by artist Joyce Burstein. It consists of a slate tombstone designed as a chalkboard, with a bronze chalk-box inviting visitors to write their own epitaphs. The project explores themes of mortality, life, and self-discovery.

name: The Epitaph Project
text:
The Epitaph Project › Background

In 1995, Burstein lived nearby and frequented what was then Hollywood Memorial Park, now Hollywood Forever. The cemetery is the final resting place for many Hollywood legends, including Rudolph Valentino, Mel Blanc, Judy Garland, and Johnny Ramone. Still it had fallen into disrepair and faced financial struggles as it neared its 100th year. During this time, salespeople eager to make a sale offered Burstein a 6x3x9-ft-deep plot at the back of the cemetery for a $68.83 monthly mortgage. Agreeing to the terms, Burstein purchased the plot.

After receiving funds from grants and fellowships, Burstein purchased a solid slate headstone and smoothed its surface to a chalkboard quality. She then had a bronze box made to hold chalk and an eraser, inviting visitors to write their own epitaphs on the slate. Finally, both the headstone and the box were installed at the empty grave plot Burstein had bought to prompt visitors to contemplate life’s impermanence. As Burstein said, “There’s something clarifying about composing or even thinking about one’s own epitaph. There can be a sense of self-discovery as well as both humor and high seriousness.”

Due to the artwork's ephemeral nature, Burstein began documenting the diverse content of visitors' responses as they considered their own epitaphs. Building on this, she assembled a collection of photos documenting the public's interaction with The Epitaph Project. As an extension of the work, Burstein shared those images on a now-defunct website, epitaphproject.com. In addition to an artist's book of the same name, which includes an essay by the philosopher and poet Peter Lamborn Wilson on the transitory nature of the graveyard space and its relationship to Burstein’s project.

name: Park 101
text:
Park 101

Park 101 is a proposed linear park on a freeway cap over US Highway 101 in downtown Los Angeles, California, US. The Los Angeles Times has compared it to Central Park, Millennium Park, and the National Mall.

name: Park 101
text:
Park 101 › History

Park 101, originally proposed as a 10-acre (40,000 m2), 0.5-mile (0.80 km) long linear park located on a freeway cap over U.S. 101 between Grand Avenue and the Los Angeles River in downtown Los Angeles, was first conceived by Nick Patsaouras in the mid-1990s. It was re-conceived with a shorter length (between Grand Avenue and east of Alameda Street) in 2008 and presented as a temporary exhibit at the Caltrans museum the following year. The purpose of the park, in addition to adding much needed greenspace to downtown Los Angeles, is to reconnect several destinations currently divided by US 101, including City Hall, the Civic Center, Union Station, Chinatown, and El Pueblo de Los Ángeles. Several new buildings were also proposed in the re-conceived project, most notably a skyscraper that if built would be the tallest building on the west coast of the United States. The Los Angeles Times compared the re-conceived project to Central Park in New York City, Millennium Park in Chicago, and the National Mall in Washington D.C.. Its estimated cost was $800 million ($1.2 billion in 2025).

In 2013, Los Angeles City Council agreed to partner with the non-profit Friends of Park 101 to search for funding for the project. In 2017, park supporters released a scaled back proposal consisting of four capped blocks between Grand Avenue and Los Angeles Street. The proposal also recommends closing several freeway on and off-ramps and developing six city and county owned sites near the park to help fund park maintenance. The estimated cost of this proposal was $180 million ($236 million in 2025).

name: The Museum of History, Science, and Art
text:
The Museum of History, Science, and Art

The Museum of History, Science, and Art was a museum in Los Angeles, California from 1913 until 1961 when it split into two institutions, Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County and Los Angeles County Museum of Art. It was stronger in its natural history holdings, but as an art museum, it organized loan exhibitions of Francisco Goya, Vincent Van Gogh, Rubens and Leonardo da Vinci.
heading_path: The Museum of History, Science, and Art

name: The Museum of History, Science, and Art
text:
The Museum of History, Science, and Art › History

In the 1890s, William Miller Bowen started a campaign to change the nature of what is now Exposition Park. There were saloons, gambling and other vice-related activity happening in the part. In 1909, Bowen's campaign succeeded in enacting a three-part ownership of the park between the state of California, Los Angeles County and the City of Los Angeles. The County agreed to develop and build a history and art museum.

Construction on the museum began, with a cornerstone laid in a ceremony officiated by the Grand Lodge Masons of California, and attended by Bowen, Los Angeles Mayor George Alexander and future California Governor William Stephens.

Four local organizations filled the galleries of the new museum: the Historical Society of Southern California, Cooper Ornithological Club, Southern California Academy of Sciences and the Fine Arts League. In 1913, the Museum was given exclusive rights to prehistoric remains from the La Brea Tar Pits, then called Rancho La Brea.

The Museum of History, Science, and Art opened on November 6, 1913 in Exposition Park.. The original building was completed in 1912 and is in the Spanish Renaissance style, with Romanesque and Beaux Arts elements as well. The architects were Frank Hudson and William A.D. Munsell. The opening festivities lasted two weeks and coincided with the opening of the Owens River Aqueduct and U.S. Senator John D. Works said that a fountain at the museum site commemorated the aqueduct.

The museum received donations of art from William Randolph Hearst and Hollywood legend Buddy DeSylva among others. In 1951, Hearst's will provided for income to benefit the museum.
heading_path: The Museum of History, Science, and Art › History

name: The Museum of History, Science, and Art
text:
The Museum of History, Science, and Art › Split

In 1961, the museum split into two entities: what is now the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

Edward W. Carter helped orchestrate the fundraising effort for the new art museum in response to J. Paul Getty's increasing reluctance to donate any more artworks to the museum. Getty had donated a few excellent artworks such as the Ardabil Carpet and Rembrandt's Portrait of Martin Looten, but then became aware of their shabby and disorganized presentation in the county's aging multipurpose museum and chose to establish his own art museum next to his house.

As to how to separate art objects from history and science objects, beginning in 1957, Richard F. Brown, who was to become the first director of LACMA and famed collector Norton Simon began to separate the art that would be part of the new art museum.
heading_path: The Museum of History, Science, and Art › Split

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street

The Los Angeles & Santa Fe Railroad Locomotive Repair Building (commonly known by its address 516 South Anderson Street, and historically tied to the Salt Lake Route) is a historic industrial building in the Boyle Heights neighborhood of Los Angeles, California, United States. Constructed in 1917 for the San Pedro, Los Angeles & Salt Lake Railroad, it is one of the last surviving early‑20th‑century locomotive repair facilities in the region and retains original industrial features including embedded shop tracks, timber trusses, and a concrete arrowhead emblem on its east facade. Historians note that the "Santa Fe" reference in municipal surveys is likely a clerical error on official archival paperwork, and the facility would have historically operated as the Los Angeles & Salt Lake Locomotive Repair Building.

After its acquisition by a private commercial trust in 1998, the building transitioned from industrial use to a dedicated filming and event facility. Its large open floor plan, elevated catwalks, and heavy‑duty structural framing made it suitable for major productions, beginning with Fox's 1998 television specials Breaking the Magician's Code: Magic's Biggest Secrets Finally Revealed. The property has since been used for a wide range of film and television projects, including 24, Inception, Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., The Colony, and the first three seasons of Lucha Underground, where it was presented on‑screen as "The Temple."

Today, 516 South Anderson Street continues to operate as a commercial studio and live event venue. It remains a notable filming location in Los Angeles and is identified by HistoricPlacesLA as potentially eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places, the California Register of Historical Resources, and as a contributor to a local industrial historic district.

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › History › Railroad origins

Constructed in 1917, the facility is officially designated in municipal surveys as the Los Angeles & Santa Fe Railroad Locomotive Repair Building, though it was historically built for and operated by the San Pedro, Los Angeles & Salt Lake Railroad. The building served as a heavy locomotive repair shop and still retains an original concrete Salt Lake Route arrowhead logo near the apex of its east facade. After Union Pacific's acquisition of the line in 1921, the site utilized a network of rail spurs extending west from the main line for industrial access. The 54,711-square-foot (5,082.8 m2) brick-and-timber structure is identified as the only remaining early-20th-century locomotive repair shop in Boyle Heights and contributes to the potential 500–600 South Anderson Street Industrial District.
heading_path: 516 South Anderson Street › History › Railroad origins

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › History › Locomotive maintenance (1917–1950s)

Designed as a fully equipped heavy repair facility, the building housed interior rail spurs, embedded shop tracks, and specialized equipment for servicing the Salt Lake Route's locomotive fleet. Its two-story industrial layout supported major mechanical work, including boiler servicing, wheel and axle repairs, and structural maintenance of locomotive frames and tender cars. The shop's concrete-floor rail alignments, still visible today, were used to move engines through different repair stations and accommodate early 20th-century maintenance practices.

Top-down aerial photography captured on May 31, 1956, confirms that the building's specialized rail infrastructure remained active into the late 1950s, visibly capturing a locomotive utilizing the curved spur tracks directly entering the western facade.
heading_path: 516 South Anderson Street › History › Locomotive maintenance (1917–1950s)

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › History › Transition to studio and media production (1997–present)

Following decades of industrial use, the property was purchased by a private commercial real estate trust on October 14, 1998, for conversion into a media production facility. Before its adaptation for filming, the building housed industrial apparel and logistics tenants, including Style Clothing Supply, Inc. and Packaging & Display USA (SCS), which operated across 510 and 516 South Anderson Street. This association contributed to the building's later nickname, the "SCS Warehouse." The property was quickly adopted by location scouts due to its large interior volume, unreinforced masonry, and high clearance.
heading_path: 516 South Anderson Street › History › Transition to studio and media production (1997–present)

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › History › Transition to studio and media production (1997–present) › Breaking the Magician's Code era (1997, 1998, 2008)

The facility's first major production occurred in late 1997 and continued into 1998, serving as the primary set for Fox's television specials Breaking the Magician's Code: Magic's Biggest Secrets Finally Revealed. Its intact industrial infrastructure provided practical utility for film crews. Original overhead catwalks and crane support systems functioned as built‑in platforms for lighting, rigging, and camera work, reducing the need for temporary scaffolding. The exterior facade occasionally retained scenic elements created for productions, including a painted advertisement reading "Apex Fuel Supply Co." which can be seen in the Levitating from the Warehouse Roof to the Ground illusion from episode 3 of the 2008 series.

Nash Entertainment used the building's interior as the setting for the series. Performer Val Valentino, appearing as the "Masked Magician," used the warehouse floor plan to demonstrate and reveal the mechanics behind large‑scale stage illusions. The building's elevated catwalks and open timber framing allowed camera crews to capture high‑angle views of illusion apparatuses, including escape doors, false floors, and mirror systems.

Although the series presents the location as a single "secret warehouse," the exterior shown in the 1998 opening credits is not 516 South Anderson Street. The establishing shot features the former Van de Kamp Bakery Building in Glassell Park, a Dutch Revival industrial landmark frequently used in Los Angeles filming. Once the camera transitions inside, however, all interior sequences were filmed at 516 South Anderson Street. The two buildings are approximately 4.5 miles apart, with the Van de Kamp building used for the exterior establishing shot and three large outdoor illusions from the 1998 specials including, Vanishing Tank (episode 3), Buried Alive (episode 4), and Death Trap (episode 4), while 516 South Anderson Street provided the interior setting.

For the 2008 MyNetworkTV revival, several illusions were staged in exterior areas of 516 South Anderson Street, including "Levitating from the Warehouse Roof to the Ground" (episode 3), "Passing Car Registration Through Car Windshield" (episode 4), and "Surviving Being Cut Up in a Wood Chipper" (episode 5).
heading_path: 516 South Anderson Street › History › Transition to studio and media production (1997–present) › Breaking the Magician's Code era (1997, 1998, 2008)

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › History › Transition to studio and media production (1997–present) › Colony era (2009)

In early 2009, the warehouse served as the primary setting and production base for the first season of the Discovery Channel series The Colony. Ten participants were housed inside the facility for 21 days to simulate post-apocalyptic survival and community reconstruction. The building's weathered masonry, deteriorated windows, and industrial condition provided the required visual aesthetic without major modification.

Production crews added scenic distressing to the exterior, including a painted advertisement reading "Apex Fuel Supply Co." Participants used interior spaces and available scrap materials to construct improvised infrastructure such as water filtration systems, small solar arrays, and security barriers.
heading_path: 516 South Anderson Street › History › Transition to studio and media production (1997–present) › Colony era (2009)

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › History › Transition to studio and media production (1997–present) › Lucha Underground Temple era (2014–2017)

Between 2014 and 2017, the facility served as the primary arena and production headquarters for the first three seasons of Lucha Underground, where it was branded on-screen as "The Temple." Produced by Mark Burnett and Robert Rodriguez, the series combined lucha libre wrestling with scripted cinematic vignettes.

Audience seating was installed in multi-tiered bleachers positioned against the brick walls surrounding the ring. Because the original timber trusses could not support broadcast lighting, crews constructed a free-standing steel rigging structure over the ring. An auxiliary office was converted into the set for the character Dario Cueto (portrayed by Luis Fernández-Gil). The industrial catwalks were incorporated into action sequences, with performers occasionally using the railings during staged stunts. Additional backstage scenes were filmed in the building's locker rooms, stairwells, and exterior alleys. Production relocated for the fourth season in 2018 to a warehouse on Industrial Street known as "The Ice Temple."
heading_path: 516 South Anderson Street › History › Transition to studio and media production (1997–present) › Lucha Underground Temple era (2014–2017)

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › Location

516 South Anderson Street is located in the eastern portion of the Boyle Heights neighborhood of Los Angeles, within a long‑established industrial corridor adjacent to the Los Angeles River. The property sits approximately 2 miles (3.2 km) east of Downtown Los Angeles and occupies a parcel within the 500–600 South Anderson Street Industrial District, a grouping of early‑20th‑century brick and timber industrial buildings historically served by the Salt Lake Route and later the Union Pacific Railroad.

The surrounding area is characterized by large warehouse structures, rail‑served lots, and heavy industrial zoning that has supported manufacturing, logistics, and later film production. The building lies near major transportation routes including the Santa Monica Freeway (I‑10), Mission Road, and the 6th Street Viaduct, providing convenient access for production vehicles and equipment.

The former Van de Kamp Bakery building in Glassell Park, located approximately 4.5 miles north of 516 South Anderson Street, has occasionally been associated with the site due to its use as an exterior establishing shot in the 1998 opening credits of Breaking the Magician's Code. Despite this visual connection, all interior filming for the series occurred at 516 South Anderson Street.

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › Architecture

The building is a prominent example of early-20th-century utilitarian railroad architecture, constructed in 1917 using a heavy concrete and steel frame beneath a two-story gabled roof. The layout was specifically designed to accommodate large-scale locomotive servicing, featuring a sprawling footprint with a multi-level main hall.

While the primary western facade was later altered covering the originally open elevation where locomotives entered with corrugated metal—the eastern elevation retains a high level of historical integrity. This eastern facade prominently features a surviving concrete arrowhead logo belonging to the Salt Lake Route, confirming Sanborn map evidence of the building's original rail operations.

name: 516 South Anderson Street
text:
516 South Anderson Street › Preservation status

The property is recognized by HistoricPlacesLA as an architecturally distinctive example of industrial development in Boyle Heights tied to regional transportation improvements between 1913 and 1945. Survey evaluations have designated the structure with multiple historic registry eligibility rankings:

National Register of Historic Places (Status Code 3B): Eligible for individual listing as a key example of railroad architecture in Los Angeles, as well as a contributing structure to the potential 500–600 South Anderson Street Industrial District under Criteria A and C.

California Register of Historical Resources (Status Code 3CB): Eligible for individual listing and as a contributor to a state-eligible historic district under Criteria 1 and 3.

Municipal Designation (Status Code 5B): Eligible for local designation as a district contributor and as an individual City of Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument.

name: Pico Union Project
text:
Pico Union Project

The Pico Union Project is a multi-faith cultural arts center and house of worship in the Pico-Union neighborhood of Downtown Los Angeles, California. Founded in 2013 by musician Craig Taubman and educator Louise Brent Taubman, the nonprofit occupies the oldest surviving synagogue building in Los Angeles and is dedicated to the principle of "love your neighbor as yourself." The organization hosts worship for Jewish, Christian, and Muslim congregations alongside concerts, cultural programming, and neighborhood social services, and its sanctuary also operates as a live music venue.

name: Pico Union Project
text:
Pico Union Project › Building

The organization's home at 1153 Valencia Street is a Greek Revival building constructed in 1909 as the first location of Sinai Temple, the city's first Conservative congregation. It is the oldest surviving synagogue building in Los Angeles and was designated Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument No. 173 in 1977. When Sinai Temple moved westward in the mid-1920s, the Welsh Presbyterian Church purchased the building, preserving its Stars of David stained glass windows, and occupied it for 88 years. The congregation seismically retrofitted the structure in the 1980s at its own expense rather than allow it to be condemned. By 2012 its membership had dwindled to roughly ten people, and after a final service that December, the dissolving congregation approached the Jewish Historical Society of Southern California about returning the building to the Jewish community. The sanctuary retains its original stained glass windows, hardwood floors, and pipe organ, with movable pews that allow the room to be reconfigured for concerts and events; it holds fewer than 400 people.

name: Pico Union Project
text:
Pico Union Project › History

At the urging of Steve Sass of the Jewish Historical Society, Craig and Louise Taubman purchased the building in 2013. Craig Taubman, then best known for the long-running Friday Night Live musical Shabbat service at Sinai Temple, initially planned a downtown performing arts venue for touring musicians. At his daughter's suggestion, the Taubmans first spent roughly six months consulting neighborhood residents, who identified housing, employment, food, health care, and safe gathering space as their most pressing needs. The couple reconceived the project as a nonprofit multi-faith cultural arts center serving the surrounding community, which is largely made up of immigrant families from Central America, Mexico, Cuba, and Korea. The Taubmans retained personal ownership of the building, initially donating its use to the nonprofit before phasing in rental payments from the organization, which retains rental income from resident faith communities, cultural groups, and private events.

By 2015, the building housed four resident faith-based organizations, three Christian and one Muslim; the Sanctuary@Pico Union program, launched that year with Jewish High Holy Day services, restored a Jewish worship presence. In 2016, Sanctuary@Pico Union received a $200,000 grant from the Jewish Community Foundation of Los Angeles, and in 2018 Zach Lasker was appointed the organization's first executive director. In November 2025, the Taubmans announced they would step down from daily leadership while remaining involved with the organization, and Serena Oberstein was named interim executive director.

name: Pico Union Project
text:
Pico Union Project › Programs

The Pico Union Project hosts regular worship for multiple faith communities, including services of the Women's Mosque of America, which held its first Friday prayer service in the building in 2015.

The organization operates Vida Sana, a free weekly farmers' market distributing fresh produce to the neighborhood's low-income residents, along with classes and professional development workshops. During the 2020 George Floyd protests, the building served as a staging ground for community activism and neighborhood support efforts. The organization also works with unhoused residents and immigrant families in the surrounding neighborhood.

name: Pico Union Project
text:
Pico Union Project › Music venue

Alongside its community programming, the sanctuary operates as an intimate concert venue. Courtney Barnett previewed her album Tell Me How You Really Feel there in 2018, in a show where the pews were removed for a standing-room audience. Rex Orange County chose the room for a surprise album-release show in 2024. The Los Angeles Chamber Orchestra has performed in the space, and the venue also hosts private events such as weddings and celebrations, with rental income supporting the nonprofit's community programs.

name: Fox Studio Lot
text:
Fox Studio Lot

The Fox Studio Lot, also known as Fox Studios, is a film and television production complex located in the Century City neighborhood of Los Angeles, California. Owned by Fox Corporation, the complex is home to the Fox Network Center, a broadcast facility for the Fox television network. The center also serves as the headquarters and flagship studio production facility for Fox Sports, including Fox Sports 1, Fox Sports 2, Fox Sports Interactive Media, and Fox Deportes. The studio lot features 80 buildings, including soundstages, backlot sets, television production and programming facilities, executive offices and support facilities.

The complex was originally the historic home of the 20th Century Fox film studio, housing the studio's production and broadcasting facilities as well as those of its subsequent corporate divisions, including 20th Television, 20th Television Animation, FX Networks, and Searchlight Pictures. Following Disney's acquisition of these assets on March 20, 2019, the divisions eventually relocated to the Walt Disney Studios lot complex in Burbank, six years after the acquisition.

The complex also formerly housed broadcasting facilities for Fox Sports Networks which departed in 2012.

name: Fox Studio Lot
text:
Fox Studio Lot › History

The complex first opened in 1928 as Fox Movietone City, after William Fox acquired 99 acres from Janss Investment Compnay and Tom Mix in 1924 and to establish a production facility for the Fox Film Corporation. Stage 6 was built in 1930. Fox Film merged with Twentieth Century Pictures in 1935, forming 20th Century-Fox. At its peak, the lot covered 285 acres.

In the 1950s, 20th Century-Fox president Spyros Skouras began to sell parcels of the lot to offset the studio's debts, which worsened during the production of Cleopatra (1963). In 1960, Skouras auctioned 176 acres of the lot's northern property; the following year William Zeckendorf and the Aluminum Company of America purchased the land from 20th Century-Fox for $43 million and demolished the on-site soundstages and bungalows. That land was developed into Century City, a corporate, retail, and residential district of Los Angeles whose name was derived from that of the studio.

In 1967, the backlot’s New York Street was constructed for the production of Hello, Dolly! (1969), after filming on location in modern-day New York City was deemed impractical for a story set in the 1890s. The set took four months to build and cost an estimated $2.25 million. Like many film sets, New York Street was originally intended to be temporary; however, the studio sought to recoup its investment by preserving the streetscape and leasing it to other studios for filming. Over the years, the set has appeared in numerous films and television productions, including Up the Sandbox (1972), New York, New York (1977), Charlie’s Angels (1976–1981), and Moonlighting (1985–1989).

Following the launch of the Fox Broadcasting Company in 1986, the network had maintained offices at the complex while retaining its primary Los Angeles offices at Metromedia Square in Los Angeles. Following the expiration of the network's lease, Fox moved its television network headquarters to the complex beginning in 1997. In 1998, Fox Sports moved its headquarters to the complex along with Fox Sports Net.

name: Fox Studio Lot
text:
Fox Studio Lot › History

Following the launch of the Fox Broadcasting Company in 1986, the network had maintained offices at the complex while retaining its primary Los Angeles offices at Metromedia Square in Los Angeles. Following the expiration of the network's lease, Fox moved its television network headquarters to the complex beginning in 1997. In 1998, Fox Sports moved its headquarters to the complex along with Fox Sports Net.

Following the completion of The Walt Disney Company's acquisition of 21st Century Fox, the company retained the complex as part of a seven-year lease. Since 2021, the complex's Fox Network Center exists in a disaster recovery role for the master control operations of Fox's national sports and entertainment networks, which are primarily transmitting from the Fox Technology Center in Tempe, Arizona.

On March 16, 2023, Fox announced the Fox Future Studio Lot project which would redevelop parts of the complex to construct new production facilities and an office complex. As part of the investment, New York Street was completely rebuilt, combining the architectural character of mid-20th-century Lower Manhattan with modern production capabilities. The redesigned set includes electrical conduits connected to the studio’s power supply to avoid the use of generators, as well as thousands of square feet of integrated interior space behind the exterior façades, allowing productions to seamlessly film both inside and outside the structures.

On April 1, 2025, Disney announced that it would vacate the complex by the end of the year, bringing 20th Century Studios’ 97-year presence and relationship with the lot to an end.

In November 2025, Fox announced plans to split up the complex as part of a $1.5 billion redevelopment plan to construct nine new soundstages along with upgrades to several production facilities and to construct an office tower as part of its Fox Future project. During the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the Fox Studio Lot served as a broadcasting hub for Fox Sports' coverage of the tournament.

name: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple
text:
Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple

Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple, formerly Hongwanji Buddhist Church of Los Angeles, also known as Nishi Hongwanji Buddhist Temple and Nishi Hompa Hongwanji Los Angeles Betsuin, is a Japanese Buddhist temple located in Los Angeles, California. The temple's second location was the first Buddhist temple in Los Angeles, one of the biggest and most influential in the United States, and is both a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument and a contributing property in the National Register of Historic Places-listed Little Tokyo Historic District.
heading_path: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple

name: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple
text:
Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › Organization

Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple is part of the Jodo Shinshu Hongwanji-ha.
heading_path: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › Organization

name: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple
text:
Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History

In the early 1900s, Los Angeles County's Japanese population was estimated to be more than 15,000, located primarily around Little Tokyo. The first Japanese Buddhist group in the area was Rafu Bukkyokai in 1904, followed by Nanka Bukkyokai (Buddhist Association of Southern California) in 1905 and Chuo Bukkyokai in 1912. The groups soon began feuding, so Kyoto's Nishi Hongan-ji sent Reverend Shuye Sonoda to mediate. Sonda merged the three groups several months later, the merger officially ratified on September 30, 1917. The name of the merged group was Hongwanji Buddhist Church of Los Angeles and their reverend was Reverend Koyu Uchida from Nanka Bukkyokai. A merger ceremony was held on April. 17, 1920.
heading_path: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History

name: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple
text:
Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › First location

Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple was first located on the second floor of Yamato Hall on Jackson Street. The temple had more than 2,000 members in 1924.
heading_path: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › First location

name: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple
text:
Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › Second location

Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple's second location, 355–369 East First Street and 109–119 North Central Avenue in downtown Los Angeles, was designed by local architect Edgar Cline and built at a cost of $185,000 in 1925 ($3.4 million in 2025). It was the first Buddhist Temple in Los Angeles, one of the largest and most influential in the United States, and was dedicated in a ceremony presided over by Lord Abbott Sonyu Ōtani with more than 1,000 in attendance on November 12, 1925. The temple was elevated to Betsuin status in 1931, the first temple in the mainland United States to do so.

The temple's assembly hall was a focal point for the neighborhood. Many cultural functions were held there, as were English language classes and the final round of the Japanese language schools oratorical competition. In 1934, the temple had 1,500 members and an operating budget of $14,000 ($336,940 in 2025).

In 1942, the temple was closed and the staff excepting Reverend Julius Goldwater were forced into internment camps. While closed, the temple stored its interned members' household goods; it also served as a hostel after the internments were lifted. The temple reopened on September 24, 1945 and had 2300 members in 1955.

The temple moved to a new location in 1969 and this building was sold to the City of Los Angeles in 1973. The building was listed as a contributing property in the National Register of Historic Places-listed Little Tokyo Historic District on August 22, 1986 and declared Los Angeles Historic Cultural Monument No. 313 on October 24 of that same year. The Japanese American National Museum moved into the building in 1992, and the following year, they received the National Preservation Honor Award for their work restoring the building.
heading_path: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › Second location

name: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple
text:
Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › Second location › Architecture and design

Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple's second location features an eclectic East Asian Exotic Revival design that combines eastern and western architectural elements. The building consists of three sections that curve around a street corner, a portion of which is commercial space that is Vernacular in design and reminiscent of traditional architecture from the west. The temple's offices, located in the northern-most portion of the building, repeat the commercial space design.

The building's First Street facade curves around the corner of First Street and Central Avenue. It features common bond-laid dark red brick on its first and second stories, while the third story is finished in plaster scored to simulate stone. The facade is topped by narrow cornice and also features a stringcourse between the second and third stories. The first floor storefronts feature glass paneled doors, transom windows, and checkerboard bulkheads made of black and yellow tiles, while the second and third stories feature symmetrically spaced double hung windows. The west end of the facade also features an office entry with a terra cotta surround and a sword and shield ornament above it. Additionally, the building's corner storefront features a wood-framed glass door with geometric muntin patterns recessed between two free-standing pillars, side windows above checkered bulkheads pierced by metal lattice vents.

The building's Central Avenue is framed by massive raised pylon-like bays that are faced by scored concrete. The temple entrance is in the south bay and features a large cement karahafu on elaborate brackets, replicating Nishi Hongan-ji's imperial gateway. Sawn wood ornaments are located on a beam under the karahafu, and above the karahafu is a window and geometric fretwork of muntins. The north bay contains the same window and muntins design; below this is a single narrow window and below that, a less elaborate ground-floor entrance that features a tapered, unadorned frame and extended lintel. Between these bays, the facade is articulated by four brick piers atop a one story brick base; each pier is two stories in height, has a patterned base and lotus-designed capital, features Egyptian motifs, and is set against a scored concrete surface. The facade's roofline features cavetto cornice and the center also features a patterned terra cotta parapet.
heading_path: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › Second location › Architecture and design

name: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple
text:
Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › Second location › Architecture and design

The building's Central Avenue is framed by massive raised pylon-like bays that are faced by scored concrete. The temple entrance is in the south bay and features a large cement karahafu on elaborate brackets, replicating Nishi Hongan-ji's imperial gateway. Sawn wood ornaments are located on a beam under the karahafu, and above the karahafu is a window and geometric fretwork of muntins. The north bay contains the same window and muntins design; below this is a single narrow window and below that, a less elaborate ground-floor entrance that features a tapered, unadorned frame and extended lintel. Between these bays, the facade is articulated by four brick piers atop a one story brick base; each pier is two stories in height, has a patterned base and lotus-designed capital, features Egyptian motifs, and is set against a scored concrete surface. The facade's roofline features cavetto cornice and the center also features a patterned terra cotta parapet.

Inside, the temple's hondo was meant to be the largest in the area, and its decorations were meant to resemble Nijo Castle and Nishi Hongan-ji.
heading_path: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › Second location › Architecture and design

name: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple
text:
Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › Current location

Motivated by rumors that the city was planning to widen First Street an amount that would cut into Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple, the temple moved to a new location, 815 East First Street, in 1969. This building, designed by Tom Makino and built by Collins and McPherson, began construction on October 14, 1968 and was dedicated with more than 2,000 in attendance on November 16, 1969. The construction cost of $1.025 million ($9 million in 2025), paid for by 1,103 donors.

A Japanese garden was added to the temple complex in 1970, and multi-purpose hall was added in 1976. A large bell tower was dedicated on the temple's 75th anniversary in 1979.
heading_path: Los Angeles Hompa Hongwanji Buddhist Temple › History › Current location

name: Bank of America Building (Los Angeles)
text:
Bank of America Building (Los Angeles)

Downtown Los Angeles's Bank of America Building, also known as Hellman Bank Building, Hellman Commercial Trust and Savings Bank Building, and SB Spring, is a historic building located at 650-660 S. Spring Street and 117 W. 7th Street in downtown Los Angeles, California. It is a contributing property in the Spring Street Financial District.

name: Bank of America Building (Los Angeles)
text:
Bank of America Building (Los Angeles) › History

Downtown Los Angeles's Bank of America Building was designed by Schultz and Weaver for Isaias Hellman and built for a reputed $2.5 million in 1924 ($47 million in 2025). The building housed the Los Angeles headquarters of Bank of America from 1930 to 1972.

In 1979, the Spring Street Financial District was added to the National Register of Historic Places, with Bank of America Building listed as a contributing property in the district. The building's bank lobby was completely vacated in 1988.

Residential real estate developer Barry Shy bought this building and two others for $75 million in 2006 ($120 million in 2025). This building was converted to 174 apartments and renamed SB Spring; the bank lobby was converted to an event space.
heading_path: Bank of America Building (Los Angeles) › History

name: Bank of America Building (Los Angeles)
text:
Bank of America Building (Los Angeles) › Architecture and design

Downtown Los Angeles's Bank of America Building is twelve stories in height and was designed in a Sullivanesque/Beaux Arts Revival style. It is made of steel-reinforced concrete and faced with terra cotta and Indian limestone. The ground floor features four ionic columns.

The building's banking area features Spanish Revival marble, wood, and metal detailing, and the bank lobby features vaulted ceilings. The top floor originally contained a conference room, but its historic features were destroyed when the building was converted to residential; the room itself was converted to a rental unit.
heading_path: Bank of America Building (Los Angeles) › Architecture and design

name: Bank of America Building (Los Angeles)
text:
Bank of America Building (Los Angeles) › Filming location

Since Bank of America vacated the building, several films have shot in the building's bank lobby, including Traffic, Seven, and Blow. The building is often used to build sets and for backdrops.
heading_path: Bank of America Building (Los Angeles) › Filming location

name: Stationers Building and Annex
text:
Stationers Building and Annex

Stationers Building and Stationers Annex were historic buildings located at 523-525 S. Spring Street in downtown Los Angeles, California. They were contributing properties in the Spring Street Financial District and were demolished sometime after 2005.

name: Stationers Building and Annex
text:
Stationers Building and Annex › History

Stationers Annex was designed by Parkinson and Bergstrom for Realty Fireproof Company and built in 1913. Stationers Building was designed by W. L. Schmolle for the York Realty Company and built in 1922. Both were small scale loft buildings and were bought by the Stationers Corporation for use as a stockroom.

In 1979, the Spring Street Financial District was added to the National Register of Historic Places, with Stationers Building and Annex, the latter unnamed, listed as two different contributing properties in the district.

Stationers Building and Annex had several different owners after the Stationers Corporation. The buildings were continually modified and eventually little of their historic features remained. The buildings were vacated, then vandalism and water damage left them out of compliance with building and safety codes. The buildings were evaluated for demolition in 2004 and demolished sometime after April 2005.

In 2014, a 40-45 story, 360-unit residential tower was proposed for the site. Prior proposals for the site included a parking garage to serve Spring Street Arcade and a twelve-story mixed use development.

name: Stationers Building and Annex
text:
Stationers Building and Annex › Architecture and design

Stationers Building and Annex were three stories in height and made of reinforced concrete. The Annex was one of the narrowest buildings in the area.

Stationers Building featured a brick facade decorated with terra cotta detailing, while the Annex's original facade was replaced by a plain stucco facade. Both buildings originally had cornice, which was removed prior to 1979.

name: San Fernando Valley
text:
Los Angeles › San Fernando Valley

The San Fernando Valley, known locally as the Valley, is an urbanized valley in Los Angeles County, California. Situated to the north of the Los Angeles Basin, it comprises a large portion of Los Angeles, the incorporated cities of Burbank, Calabasas, Glendale, Hidden Hills and San Fernando, plus several unincorporated areas. It has a population of about 1.8 million spread over 260 square miles (670 km2). The valley is the home of Warner Bros. Studios, Walt Disney Studios, and the Universal Studios Hollywood theme park.

text: Los Angeles in January: typical highs 19 °C and lows 7 °C, about 68 mm of rain spread over about 5 days with at least 1 mm (1996 to 2025 averages, Open-Meteo reanalysis).

name: Los Angeles climate in March

name: Art Deco L.A.: Zigzags, Spires, and Stories
text:
Art Deco L.A.: Zigzags, Spires, and Stories — walking tour by Los Angeles Conservancy in Los Angeles, paid.
A Downtown Los Angeles architecture walk focused on 1920s and 1930s Art Deco, including geometric facades, historic interiors and the craftsmanship behind the city's landmark buildings.
Meeting point: Pershing Square, 532 S Olive St, Los Angeles, CA 90013. Starts: Saturdays at 10:15. Duration: about 2 h. Languages: English.
Free registration on the operator's website is required.
address: 532 S Olive St, Los Angeles, CA 90013

name: Curtains Up on Broadway: L.A.'s Historic Theatre District
text:
Curtains Up on Broadway: L.A.'s Historic Theatre District — walking tour by Los Angeles Conservancy in Los Angeles, paid.
